subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Scorching and Tipping
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Scorching and Tipping.

hook.text: Scorched beans have dark burn marks on their flat faces. Tipped beans have blackened edges. Both ruin the cup.

buildup.text: Scorching happens when the drum is too hot at charge (when green beans are added). The surface burns on contact.

discovery.text: Tipping occurs when beans overheat at the thin edges during late roast stages—the weakest parts blacken first.

twist.text: Both defects taste smoky, acrid, and bitter. They're often mistaken for 'bold' flavor by untrained palates.

climax.text: Preventing them requires proper charge temperature, drum speed, and batch size. They're equipment and technique problems.

punchline.text: Dark spots on the bean, bitter notes in the cup. The drum was too aggressive.

quiz.question: What causes scorching during roasting?
options: The drum being too hot when green beans are first added

details.summary: Scorching leaves dark burn marks on the flat surfaces of beans, while tipping chars the pointed ends. Both defects occur when the drum or charge temperature is too high at the start of the roast. They introduce harsh, carbon-like flavors that cannot be corrected.
details.whyItMatters: Scorching and tipping are irreversible defects that ruin batches. Recognizing their causes helps roasters prevent costly mistakes and maintain cup quality.
takeaways: Scorching burns flat bean surfaces from excessive contact heat
Tipping chars the pointed tips of each bean
Both result from too-high charge temperature at the roast start

faq.question: How can a roaster prevent scorching and tipping in a drum roaster?
faq.answer: Lower the charge temperature, ensure adequate drum speed for tumbling, and reduce gas input during the first minutes. Pre-heating the drum evenly and using appropriate batch sizes also help prevent direct surface burns.

faq.question: Can scorched or tipped beans be identified visually before brewing?
faq.answer: Yes. Scorching appears as dark patches or streaks on the flat side of the bean, while tipping shows as blackened or charred tips. Sorting these out during quality control improves the overall batch flavor.
